# E5 — is the GPU working, or waiting to be given work?

**Generated by `bench/make_e5_report.py` from the committed `timeline_summary.csv` files.** Nothing here is typed in.

A phase can be slow for three different reasons and only one of them is a memory problem. E5 separates the third: time when the GPU has **nothing queued**, because the host has not yet launched the next kernel. That time is invisible to `ncu` — which profiles kernels, and an idle GPU runs none — so it cannot be found in Part C's data at any resolution.

**Read `gpu_idle_frac_corrected` where it exists.** nsys's own tracing stretches each region by roughly ×1.53 on this device, so the raw fraction overstates idleness. Both are shown.

## Did the per-region split survive this capture?

A capture taken through `--compile-mode` has no NVTX regions: the context managers graph-break the model, so it runs `--no-regions` and reports one `whole_capture` row. A capture taken through a ladder `--rung` keeps its regions, because the rungs compile `embed_image`, `container.forward` and `denoise_step` individually and the instrumentation goes on afterwards. A single-row run below means the first thing happened — not that the phases had no kernels.

## What this means for a memory-side accelerator

The idle fraction is the share of the phase during which **no kernel is running at all**. It bounds what a change can deliver — but only a change of a particular kind, and the distinction matters:

* A design that makes each kernel **faster** without changing how many there are cannot touch the idle share at all. The work is not on the GPU during it. For such a change the table below is a hard ceiling.
* A design that **reduces the number of kernels** — by fusing them, or by replacing a sequence of small launches with one operation — attacks the idle time directly, because the idle time *is* the launch gaps. π0's `ae_step` issues ~968 kernels per denoising step with a 62 µs median gap; a design that issued ten would remove most of that 84 % rather than run into it.

So the ceiling below is the right number for "this kernel gets faster" and the wrong number for "this kernel stops existing". A processing-in-memory proposal can be either, and which one it is has to be stated before this table is applied to it.

| model | mode | region | idle frac (corrected where a matched unprofiled reference exists, else raw) | ceiling on any kernel-side speedup |

The right-hand column is Amdahl's law with the idle time as the serial part: even a kernel-side change that made every kernel take **zero** time would leave the idle share untouched **if the kernel count is unchanged**. For π0's eager `ae_step` — 84.3 % idle — that ceiling is 6.4×, reached only in the limit of free kernels. For the whole eager inference at N=10 it is 2.2×, because the two phases that are not dispatch-bound make up the rest of the frame. A design that also removes launches is not bound by these numbers.

This is the third independent measurement pointing the same way. Part B: no optimised configuration has an action expert that dominates its frame. E7: the expert is 55.5 % of π0's latency at N=10 but 22.4 % of its above-idle energy. E5: the expert is 84 % idle, so most of that latency is not work at all. The three are measuring different things and agree.
